# Getting the most out of Opus 5.5 in Claude and Claude Code

How to prompt Opus 5.5, steer a long run, and check your results in Claude apps and Claude Code.

Opus 5.5 works well with the way you already use Claude. A few things behave differently, though: it works for longer on its own, it tells you plainly what it did, and it thinks before every reply. This guide covers how to work with Opus 5.5 in Claude apps and Claude Code, including how to prompt the model, steer a long run, and check your results.

## TRY THIS FIRST

Three things to try in your first session with Opus 5.5

- Hand over the whole task. Say what âdoneâ looks like and when you want it to stop and ask. Then let it work.

- Delete âthink carefullyâ lines. Opus 5.5 already thinks before every reply.

- When a long run ends, read what it needs from you first.

## 1. HOW TO ASK

### Say what âdoneâ looks like, then let it run

What to do. Give the whole task in one message. Name the finish line, like âthe tests passâ or âevery endpoint is migrated.â Then let it cook.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps going on long, multi-part work better than Opus 5 did. Compared to prior Opus models, its biggest gains are on multi-step work, like carrying a change through a large repository until the tests pass. Early testers had it run long coding tasks for hours with little oversight. With a clear finish line, it knows when itâs done.

How. In Claude Code, for example:

Migrate the payment endpoints from the old client to the new one. Done means: every endpoint uses the new client, the old client is deleted, and the test suite passes. Stop and ask me only if a test fails for a reason you can't explain.

### Stop telling it to âthink hardâ

What to do. Remove âthink carefully,â âthink step by step,â and similar lines from your prompts and your saved instructions.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 always thinks before it replies, and it decides how much. You donât need to ask it to think. In our testing in a chat product, removing a âthink carefullyâ line made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.

How. Delete the line. For a quick answer to a simple question, say so: âAnswer directly.â To change how much it thinks in Claude Code, change effort.

### Add to a running task

What to do. If you remember something mid-run, you can type a follow-up while it works.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now, so a restart costs more.

How to do it. In Claude Code, type the message and press Enter while Claude works, for example, âAlso keep the old endpoint names as aliases.â

### For design work, name the styles you donât want

What to do. When you ask for a page, an app, or an artifact, list the design habits you want left out.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. With no design direction, Opus 5.5 falls back on a few default styles. A general instruction like âavoid a generic lookâ mostly swaps one default for another. A list of specific patterns works much better.

How. Name the patterns:

Build a personal website with placeholder content. Don't use a cream or off-white background, italic accent words in headings, numbered "01 / 02 / 03" section labels, monospace labels, or pill-shaped buttons.

Then look at what it chose instead. If you donât like that either, add it to the list and ask again.

## 2. STEERING A LONG RUN IN CLAUDE CODE

### Tell it which stops you want

What to do. Put a short rule in your CLAUDE.md file about when to stop and ask, and when to keep going.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 keeps you posted as it works. On a long task, it sometimes stops to report instead of going on: a summary that names the next step without taking it, an offer to continue, or a list of choices that donât block the work. It follows instructions that name these stops. Name the stops you want, too.

How. Add this to CLAUDE.md, and edit it to fit your project:

When a step doesn't need my input, keep going. Put status notes in the same message as your next action. Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository.

If a run stops with âWant me to continue?â reply âcontinue.â If that happens often, the rule above will help.

A rule to keep going means fewer stops, so keep your own check before anything risky or hard to undo. The last line of the rule above does that. Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands too.

For pair programming, you may want the opposite: a one-line plan before it starts and a short recap at the end. Say that in your CLAUDE.md instead. Opus 5.5 follows either one.

### Ask it to split big work across subagents

What to do. For an audit, a migration, or a review across a large codebase, ask Opus 5.5 to split the work across subagents and check each result.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Early testers had Opus 5.5 coordinate parallel subagents on long audits and migrations, with little oversight.

How.

Audit every service in services/ for the retry bug in the linked issue. Give each service to its own subagent. When a subagent reports back, check its evidence before you accept it. Finish with one table: service, affected yes or no, and the evidence.

### Keep the task list in a file

What to do. For a run that will take a while, ask Opus 5.5 to keep its task list in a file and update it as it goes. Then read the file, not the scrollback, to see where the run is.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Runs are longer now. A long run fills the context window, and Claude Code then summarizes older turns. A list in a file survives that, and it shows you at a glance whatâs done and whatâs left.

How. âKeep a checklist in TASKS.md. Tick each item when itâs done, and add anything new you find.â

## 3. CHECKING THE RESULT

### Read what it needs from you first

What to do. When a long run ends, look first for anything Claude is waiting on you for, like a decision it left open or a change it wants you to approve. Then read the rest of Claudeâs summary.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reports on its work more clearly than Opus 5. Its updates and its final summary say what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you, in plain language.

How. To change the summaryâs format, say so in CLAUDE.md, for example, âEnd every run with three headings: Blocked on me, Changed, Found.â

### Ask it to review the code

What to do. Ask Opus 5.5 to review a diff or a pull request before a person does.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. One early tester said Opus 5.5 at its lowest effort caught more bugs than Opus 5 at high effort, with fewer false alarms. It also explains its changes in plain language, so its pull request descriptions are easier to review.

How. Feed this prompt to Claude:

Review the diff on this branch against main. List only problems you'd block the merge for. For each one, give the file and line, why it's wrong, and how to show it fails.

### Ask it to mark what it couldnât confirm

What to do. For research and analysis, ask it to say what it couldnât find or couldnât check.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. âI couldnât find thisâ is worth reading, and asking for it makes it easy to find.

How. Add âMark anything you couldnât confirm, and say where you lookedâ to the request. This works in a Claude research report and in Claude Code.

## 4. IN CLAUDE APPS

First, check that the model picker says Opus 5.5.

### Share the chart or screenshot itself

What to do. Attach the chart, diagram, screenshot, or slide. Donât retype the numbers.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 reads charts, diagrams, and screenshots more accurately than Opus 5, and it needs no extra steps to do it. Itâs also better at meaning that depends on where things are in the image: which boxes an arrow connects, what changed between two versions of a diagram, or when a meeting starts and ends in a calendar screenshot.

How. Attach the image and ask a specific question: âWhich of these services call the billing API directly?â

### Ask it to check a long document

What to do. Give it a long plan, report, or deck, and ask it to find mistakes.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 pays more attention to detail than prior Opus models. In our testing, it caught a date that fell on the wrong weekday in a long planning thread, and a chart that didnât match the numbers in a deck.

How. Submit the prompt: âCheck this deck for anything that contradicts itself: numbers, dates and names. Quote each problem and say where it is.â

### Ask for the finished file

What to do. When you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the file, not an outline.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. The spreadsheets and documents Opus 5.5 makes need less editing than Opus 5âs before you share them.

How. âMake this a spreadsheet I can share: one row per vendor, with columns for cost, contract end date and owner.â

### In a project, say when answers are settled

What to do. If follow-up questions in a long chat feel slow, add an instruction that earlier answers are settled.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. In a long chat, Opus 5.5 sometimes goes back over an earlier answer while it thinks about a short follow-up. That slows the reply.

How. Add this to the projectâs instructions:

Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done. Focus on what I'm asking now, and don't go back over an earlier answer unless I ask about it or point out a problem with it.

Leave it out of projects for long analysis, where a later step can show a mistake in an earlier one.

## 5. WHEN A MESSAGE IS FLAGGED

Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with Fable-level bio and cyber safeguards. In Claude apps and Claude Code, most flagged messages move to an older model, and your work goes on there. Finding security vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, and everyday health and educational questions should still work. These safeguards can sometimes flag legitimate work, and weâre tuning them to cut down on incorrect flags. If youâre switched, hereâs what youâll see and what to do.

### In Claude apps

What you see. A notice that starts with âSwitched toâ and the name of an older model. Claude answers on that model, and the chat stays on it.

What to do.

- To go back to Opus 5.5, choose it in the model picker. If the earlier message is still in the chat, it may be flagged again. Starting a new chat avoids that.

- To be asked first, go to Settings, then Capabilities, and turn off âSwitch models when a message is flagged.â Youâll see a âpausedâ card with your options.

The check covers everything in the conversation, including files and search results. So a flag can come from earlier content, not only your last message.

### In Claude Code

What you see. A notice that names the older model. The session continues on that model.

- Run /model to switch back.

- Press Esc twice to edit your last message and try again.

- To be asked first, run /config and change âSwitch models when a message is flagged.â

- Run /feedback if the flag was wrong.

### Donât ask it to show its reasoning in the reply

What to do. Remove requests to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply from your prompts and instructions.

Why it matters on Opus 5.5. A request to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply can be declined. Itâs one of the flag categories.

How. Ask Claude for what you need instead, for example, âExplain why you chose this approach in three sentences.â

## 6. SPEED

### Turn on fast mode when youâre waiting on each reply

What to do. In Claude Code, use fast mode for back-and-forth work, where you read each reply before you send the next message.

# How the Claude Code team does code review

How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.

We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

## RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

Code review does two jobs:

- Find and fix issues before they ship

- Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which checkâautomated or humanâis the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

## THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

## THE LIFE OF A CHANGE

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

## LAYER BY LAYER

### 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can runâlike tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the designâand ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide .

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

- CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.

- REVIEW.md , written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

### 2. AI review on every pull request

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code , is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview , the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

### 3. Security review that can block

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code .

### 4. Automated checks that block

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here .) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

### 5. Human approval, scaled by risk

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

### 6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.

### 7. Fast detection, fast rollback

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

## HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER

Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.

Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.

We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.

Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.

Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.

When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.

We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review:

- A round cap. After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach.

- Diff-only re-review after the first few passes.

- Flag the class of bug, so the auth
